items.blueprint: FAR.III.A Accounting Changes and Error Corrections
items.task: Account for changes in principle, estimate and reporting entity, and correct prior-period errors
items.task_source: FAR_SPEC.md 2026 Blueprint Area III groups (secondary source; AICPA original not opened; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: Which of the following is a change in accounting principle rather than a change in estimate or the correction of an error?
options: A company shortens the expected useful life of its delivery trucks after reviewing their actual usage
A company that recognized revenue only when cash was received begins recognizing it when earned
A company adopts straight-line depreciation for a newly purchased class of assets that it did not own before
A company switches its inventory cost-flow assumption from FIFO to weighted-average cost because the new method is preferable
items.rule_line: A change in principle is a switch between two acceptable methods and requires a preferability justification.

why.A: A revised useful life is a change in accounting estimate. It arises from new information about future benefits, not from choosing a different principle.
why.B: Cash-basis revenue recognition was never generally accepted. Moving to GAAP is the correction of an error, not a change in principle.
why.C: Adopting a method for a new type of transaction or event is not a change in principle because no prior method existed for that item.
why.D: Correct. Moving from one generally accepted method to another is a change in accounting principle and must be justified as preferable.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Which changes replace one accepted principle with another accepted principle?
guide.reveal: Those moving between GAAP-permitted methods, with justification of preferability.

guide.ask: Which listed situation switches an inventory cost-flow assumption from one acceptable method to another?
guide.reveal: The switch from FIFO to weighted-average.

items.stem: A company voluntarily changes an accounting principle and the change is permitted because the new principle is preferable. How does it report the change in its comparative financial statements?
options: It applies the new principle only to current and future periods and leaves the prior statements unchanged
It reports the cumulative effect as a separate line in the current-year income statement
It reports the change only in the notes, with no adjustment to any reported amount
It applies the new principle retrospectively, adjusting the opening balance of retained earnings of the earliest period presented
items.rule_line: Retrospective application is the default for voluntary changes in principle, with the cumulative effect in opening retained earnings.

why.A: Prospective application is used for changes in estimate, or when retrospective application is impracticable. It is not the default for a change in principle.
why.B: A cumulative-effect line in current income was the old treatment. Current guidance places the effect in opening retained earnings of the earliest period shown.
why.C: Disclosure alone is not enough. Prior-period amounts are adjusted, and the notes explain the nature of, and reason for, the change.
why.D: Correct. Retrospective application recasts prior periods presented as if the new principle had always been used, with the cumulative effect of earlier periods in opening retained earnings.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Does a voluntary change in principle apply to the past or only forward?
guide.reveal: It is applied retrospectively to prior periods presented.

guide.ask: Where does the cumulative effect of earlier periods go?
guide.reveal: Into the opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented.

items.stem: Sequoia Freight Inc. bought equipment for $120,000 on January 1, 2023, with an estimated 10-year life and no salvage value, and uses straight-line depreciation. On January 1, 2026, after a review, management concluded that the total life is 8 years from acquisition. What is the depreciation expense for 2026?
items.rule_line: A change in estimate is applied prospectively: remaining carrying amount less salvage over the remaining revised life.

why.A: Spreads the carrying amount over the new total life of 8 years instead of the 5 remaining years.
why.B: Keeps the old $12,000 charge. The revised life must be used from the date of the change.
why.C: Divides the original cost by the new total life. A change in estimate is applied to the carrying amount over the remaining life, not to original cost.
why.D: Correct. Carrying amount $84,000 after three years of $12,000 is spread over the 5 remaining years: $16,800.

guide.ask: What is the carrying amount at the start of 2026?
How many years remain under the revised life, and what is the depreciation?

items.stem: Harbor Point Corp. acquired machinery on January 1, 2023, for $250,000. It uses straight-line depreciation over an 8-year life with a salvage value of $10,000. On January 1, 2026, management revised the total useful life to 10 years and the salvage value to $20,000. What is 2026 depreciation expense?
items.rule_line: Revised depreciation equals carrying amount less revised salvage, divided by the remaining life, from the change date.

why.A: Correct. Carrying amount $160,000 less revised salvage $20,000 = $140,000, spread over 7 remaining years.
why.B: Uses the old salvage value. The revised salvage estimate applies from the date of the change.
why.C: Ignores salvage value entirely. Depreciable base is carrying amount less expected salvage.
why.D: Applies the new life and salvage to original cost, ignoring the three years already depreciated.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: What is the carrying amount at the start of 2026?
Apply the revised salvage and the remaining life.

items.stem: Delmar Foods Inc. voluntarily changes from LIFO to FIFO in 2026 and applies the change retrospectively. Inventory at December 31, 2025, was $560,000 under LIFO and $640,000 under FIFO. The tax rate is 25%. What is the increase in January 1, 2026, retained earnings reported for this change?
items.rule_line: The cumulative effect of a change in principle is adjusted to opening retained earnings, net of tax.

why.A: Reports only the tax effect. The adjustment is the pretax difference reduced by tax, not the tax itself.
why.B: Correct. The $80,000 higher FIFO inventory raises prior cumulative income by $80,000, less 25% tax = $60,000.
why.C: Stops at the pretax amount. Retained earnings is adjusted net of the related income tax effect.
why.D: Adds tax instead of deducting it. Higher income creates higher tax expense, which reduces the net adjustment.

guide.ask: What is the pretax difference in prior cumulative income?
guide.reveal: Higher FIFO inventory of 80,000.

guide.ask: Net of tax, what is the retained earnings increase?

items.stem: On January 1, 2025, Quill Systems Inc. paid $90,000 for equipment with a 5-year life and no salvage value, and mistakenly recorded it as repair expense. The error was found in 2026, and the 2025 statements are already issued. The tax rate is 20%. What is the net-of-tax adjustment to the opening retained earnings of 2026, assuming straight-line depreciation would have been used?
items.rule_line: A material prior-period error is corrected by restating, with the adjustment to opening retained earnings shown net of tax.

why.A: Reflects only the after-tax depreciation. The expensed cost of the asset is also reversed.
why.B: Correct. Net asset that should be on hand at 12/31/25 is $90,000 - $18,000 = $72,000; after 20% tax the retained earnings adjustment is $57,600.
why.C: Omits the tax effect. The correction to retained earnings is presented net of income tax.
why.D: Reverses the full $90,000 with no depreciation and no tax. The asset would have been depreciated for 2025 and the effect taxed.

items.stem: Tamarack Retail Inc. reported 2026 net income of $400,000. It later found that ending inventory was overstated by $30,000 at December 31, 2025, and understated by $10,000 at December 31, 2026. Ignoring income taxes, what is the correct 2026 net income?
items.rule_line: Opening inventory errors affect income opposite to the prior year; ending inventory errors affect income in the same direction as inventory.

why.A: Reverses both signs. Opening overstatement lowers income of the following year, so the correction is an increase.
why.B: Subtracts the opening error and adds the ending error, the reverse of the true effect on each.
why.C: Treats the understated ending inventory as if it overstated income. Understated ending inventory overstates cost of goods sold and lowers income.
why.D: Correct. Overstated opening inventory raised 2026 cost of goods sold, so income was understated by $30,000. Understated ending inventory raised it again by $10,000. Corrected income is $440,000.

steps: Overstated opening inventory 30,000 -> 2026 COGS too high -> income understated by 30,000
Understated ending inventory 10,000 -> 2026 COGS too high -> income understated by 10,000

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: How does an overstated opening inventory affect the year's income?
guide.reveal: It raises cost of goods sold, so income is understated by 30,000.

guide.ask: How does the understated ending inventory affect it, and what is the corrected income?
guide.reveal: Also raises cost of goods sold, income understated by 10,000; 400,000 + 30,000 + 10,000 = 440,000.

items.stem: Wexford Services Inc. did not accrue wages at year-end. Unrecorded wages payable were $12,000 at December 31, 2025, and $18,000 at December 31, 2026, and all wages were expensed when paid. Reported 2026 income before tax was $250,000. What is the corrected 2026 income before tax?
items.rule_line: Corrected expense equals expense paid, less opening accrual, plus closing accrual; an omitted accrual overstates income.

why.A: Deducts both amounts. Only the current year-end accrual reduces income; the prior accrual was paid in 2026 and belongs to 2025.
why.B: Correct. The 2025 wages paid in 2026 were wrongly expensed in 2026 (+$12,000), and the 2026 wages unpaid at year-end were omitted (-$18,000): $244,000.
why.C: Reverses both adjustments. The prior-year accrual raises 2026 income when removed; the year-end accrual lowers it.
why.D: Adds the current year-end accrual instead of deducting it. Unrecorded expense means income was overstated.

steps: 2026 expense as reported = cash paid for wages

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Which year's wages were paid and wrongly expensed in 2026?
guide.reveal: The 12,000 of 2025 wages.

guide.ask: Which year-end wages were omitted?

items.stem: In 2026, a company discovers that an error in the 2025 financial statements, which have been issued, was material. Which treatment is required?
options: Include the correction in 2026 net income as an extraordinary item
Treat it as a change in estimate and adjust only current and future periods
Disclose the error in the notes only, leaving 2025 amounts unchanged
Restate the prior-period statements and adjust opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented
items.rule_line: Material errors in issued statements are corrected by restating prior periods and disclosing the error's effects.

why.A: Errors are never corrected through current income, and extraordinary items no longer exist in US GAAP.
why.B: An error results from misuse of facts or a mistake, not from new information. It is not a change in estimate.
why.C: Disclosure without correcting the affected amounts does not satisfy the restatement requirement.
why.D: Correct. Material errors are corrected by restatement of previously issued statements, with disclosure of the nature of the error and its effect.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Is a material error in issued statements corrected in the current year or by restating?
guide.reveal: By restating the prior-period statements.

guide.ask: What happens to opening retained earnings?
guide.reveal: It is adjusted for the earliest period presented.

items.stem: A parent company changes its reporting entity by adding a previously unconsolidated subsidiary to its consolidated financial statements, because it now controls the subsidiary through common ownership changes among affiliates. How is the change reported?
options: Prospectively from the date of the change, with no restatement of prior periods
As a correction of an error in every prior period presented
As a component of income from discontinued operations in the current period
Retrospectively, by recasting the financial statements of all prior periods presented as though the new entity had been included from the start
items.rule_line: A change in reporting entity is applied retrospectively by recasting all prior periods presented.

why.A: Prospective treatment is reserved for changes in estimate. A change in reporting entity requires recasting.
why.B: The prior statements were not wrong when issued. A change in reporting entity is not an error correction.
why.C: Discontinued operations relate to disposals. Adding an entity does not create a discontinued operation.
why.D: Correct. A change in reporting entity is a special type of change in principle and is applied retrospectively to all periods presented.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: What kind of change is adding a previously unconsolidated subsidiary because of a change in the reporting entity?
guide.reveal: A special type of change in principle.

guide.ask: How is it applied?
guide.reveal: Retrospectively, recasting all prior periods presented.

Ending accounts receivable are $800,000, and the allowance has a credit balance of $10,000 before adjustment. What is bad debt expense for 2026?
items.rule_line: A revised uncollectible estimate is recognized in current expense; the allowance is brought to the newly estimated balance.

why.A: Uses the old 4% rate. The revised rate applies as of the date of the new information.
why.B: Correct. Required allowance $48,000 less existing credit balance $10,000 = $38,000. The change in estimate flows through current expense.
why.C: Ignores the existing $10,000 credit balance. Expense equals the required ending allowance less the balance already carried.
why.D: Adds the existing balance to the required allowance instead of netting it.

How does the existing balance affect the expense?

items.rule_line: A prior-period error's effect on retained earnings is stated net of the income tax effect.

why.A: Only the tax portion. The retained earnings effect is the net income overstatement after tax.
why.B: Correct. The 2025 revenue overstatement of $50,000 less the $15,000 tax effect is $35,000 lower cumulative net income at the start of 2026.
why.C: Pretax amount; the adjustment to retained earnings is net of tax.
why.D: Adds the tax to the revenue error. Lower revenue also lowers income tax, so the net effect is smaller than $50,000.

steps: Overstated 2025 revenue 50,000 with no offsetting cost

items.stem: Larch Hardware Inc. changes from LIFO to FIFO in 2026. FIFO exceeded LIFO inventory by $60,000 at December 31, 2024, and by $100,000 at December 31, 2025. The 2025 net income originally reported was $210,000, and the tax rate is 25%. In the 2026 comparative statements, what is 2025 net income after retrospective application?
items.rule_line: Restated income for a period equals reported income plus the after-tax change in the FIFO-LIFO inventory difference during that period.

why.A: Correct. The FIFO inventory rose by $40,000 during 2025, lowering 2025 cost of goods sold by $40,000. After 25% tax, income rises $30,000 to $240,000.
why.B: Adds the pretax amount. Restated income reflects the tax effect of the higher pretax income.
why.C: Uses the beginning-of-year difference instead of the change during 2025.
why.D: Uses the full year-end 2025 difference, which includes the cumulative amount from 2024. Only the change during 2025 affects 2025 income.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: How much did the FIFO-LIFO inventory difference change during 2025?
guide.reveal: 100,000 - 60,000 = 40,000, lowering 2025 cost of goods sold.

items.stem: When may a company voluntarily change from one generally accepted accounting principle to another?
options: The change lowers reported income tax expense for the period
The change is immaterial to the current year's income, whatever the reason for making it or the effect on future periods
The company has the approval of its lender
The company can justify that the new principle is preferable and it discloses the reason
items.rule_line: A voluntary change in principle is allowed only when the entity justifies the new principle as preferable.

why.A: Tax savings are not a reason for a voluntary change. Preferability is judged on the quality of financial reporting.
why.B: Immateriality of the current-year effect does not by itself justify a change in principle.
why.C: Lender approval is a contractual matter. GAAP requires a preferability justification.
why.D: Correct. A voluntary change is allowed only if the entity justifies that the alternative principle is preferable.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: What must a company show to justify a voluntary change in principle?
guide.reveal: That the new principle is preferable.

guide.ask: What must it also do?
guide.reveal: Disclose the reason for the change.

items.stem: Beacon Outfitters Inc. understated its ending inventory by $20,000 at December 31, 2025, and never discovered the error. Which describes the effect at December 31, 2026, ignoring taxes?
options: Retained earnings is understated by $20,000 because the 2025 error was not corrected in the accounts
Retained earnings is overstated by $20,000 because 2026 income is overstated
Ending 2026 inventory is understated by $20,000 as a result of the error
Retained earnings at December 31, 2026, is correct because the error reversed in 2026
items.rule_line: Ending inventory errors are counterbalancing: they misstate income in two years but retained earnings is correct after the second year.

why.A: Ignores the reversal. Opening inventory in 2026 is too low, which lowers 2026 cost of goods sold and offsets the 2025 effect.
why.B: The 2026 overstatement exactly offsets the 2025 understatement, so cumulative retained earnings is not misstated.
why.C: The 2025 error affects opening 2026 inventory only. Ending 2026 inventory is measured from the count at that date and is unaffected.
why.D: Correct. The 2025 understatement reduced 2025 income; the same amount overstated 2026 income through opening inventory, so retained earnings at the end of 2026 is correct.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Does an ending inventory error carry over to the next year?
guide.reveal: Yes, it reverses in the following year's income.

guide.ask: What is left in retained earnings at the end of the second year?
guide.reveal: Nothing; the balance is correct.

why.B: Divides the original cost by the new total life. The change in estimate applies to the remaining carrying amount.
why.C: Correct. Carrying amount $400,000 is amortized over the 6 remaining years: $66,667.

items.stem: Granite Ridge Inc. bought equipment on January 1, 2023, for $260,000 (10-year life, no salvage) and used straight-line depreciation. On January 1, 2026, it changes to double-declining balance, which is preferable, and keeps the original 10-year total life, so 7 years remain at the change date. What is depreciation expense for 2026?
items.rule_line: A depreciation method change is treated as a change in estimate effected by a change in principle, applied prospectively.

why.A: Continues straight-line. The new method is applied from the date of the change.
why.B: Applies the DDB rate of 20% (based on the original 10-year life) to the carrying amount. The rate must reflect the 7 remaining years.
why.C: Correct. A change in depreciation method is a change in estimate effected by a change in principle, applied prospectively: carrying amount $182,000 x 2/7 = $52,000.
why.D: Books a catch-up as if DDB had always been used and then adds the fourth-year DDB charge. A change in depreciation method is not applied retrospectively.

items.topic: Change to LIFO when data are unavailable
items.task: Account for changes in principle, estimate and reporting entity, and correct prior-period errors

items.stem: Meridian Metals Inc. changes its inventory method from FIFO to LIFO in 2026. Records needed to compute the effect on prior years' LIFO layers are unavailable, so retrospective application is impracticable. Which is the appropriate treatment?
options: Restate all prior years by estimating hypothetical LIFO layers from industry price indexes
Reject the change because a change to LIFO cannot be made without retrospective restatement
Report the cumulative difference between FIFO and LIFO as a gain or loss in 2026 income
Use the carrying amount of inventory at the start of 2026 as the opening LIFO base layer and apply LIFO prospectively from that date
items.rule_line: If prior-period effects are impracticable to determine, the new principle applies prospectively from the earliest practicable date.

why.A: Retrospective application is required only when practicable. Where the needed data cannot be obtained, prospective application is used.
why.B: The standard explicitly allows prospective application when retrospective application is impracticable.
why.C: Cumulative effects of a change in principle are not recognized in current-period income.
why.D: Correct. When it is impracticable to determine prior-period effects, the change to LIFO is applied prospectively with opening inventory becoming the base layer.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Can prior LIFO layers be recreated when records are unavailable?
guide.reveal: No, retrospective application is impracticable.

guide.ask: How is the change made in that case?
guide.reveal: Prospectively, with opening inventory as the base layer.

items.stem: Which description correctly distinguishes recognized subsequent events from nonrecognized subsequent events?
options: Recognized events occur before the balance sheet date; nonrecognized events occur after the auditor's report date
Recognized events are those with a favorable effect; nonrecognized events are those with an unfavorable effect
Recognized events are recorded in the notes; nonrecognized events are recorded in the accounts
Recognized events provide evidence of conditions that existed at the balance sheet date; nonrecognized events arise after that date
items.rule_line: Adjust for subsequent events that clarify conditions existing at the balance sheet date; disclose those that arise afterward.

why.B: The direction of the effect does not decide recognition.
why.C: The treatments are reversed. Recognized events adjust the accounts, and nonrecognized events are disclosed.
why.D: Correct. Recognized events give additional evidence about conditions existing at the balance sheet date and adjust the statements. Nonrecognized events concern conditions arising afterward and are disclosed if material.
